pitch_detail.notes: Face climbing at 5.11a gives way to a 5.10b left-facing corner; then slant left, which skips 40-plus feet of dirt and hummocks on the Mitten's right side, to a large corner and the Pervertical belay. Three bolts protect it. Reach the start via a fourth-class traverse leftward from beneath D7.
Follow the left-facing corner, step right around the edge into a right-facing corner and continue to the top of the Mitten.
Pass over a slot, then stem up a shaft and left-facing corner system. Traverse left past an old bolt and a fixed Friend, and belay off to the right. A long pitch.
The hard pitch of the route: a finger crack, then left past some shaky flakes, then up a sustained shallow right-facing corner and crack. The belay is a poor one on a sloping ledge out to the right.
Step left into the right-facing corner again and fight upward to the pillar's crest and a huge ledge.
Go straight up an inset section, passing a fixed pin, and finish on Table Ledge.

review.changed: Wrote all six pitches with grades and lengths (feet converted to metres). P4 grade not stated, so omitted; crux flagged because the text calls it the crux pitch. Rappel table not written: the stored descent text covers it and the source has no station list.
review.other_findings: Pitch grades in the text top out at 5.11b/c; stored route grade is 5.12a.

pitch_detail.notes: Find the pink rock band left of the giant right-facing dihedral and climb through it, then follow a grassy dihedral of the same orientation to a pleasant ledge. Slings there make the belay.

Step left from the ledge and face climb to another ledge, step right and go up a left-facing dihedral toward a white roof. Pass the roof on its right and belay on very small gear. The alternative goes straight up the dihedral to a belay above the roof and to the right, near a slung block holding a retreat anchor.

A serious slab (5.8) angles up and left to the base of a big dihedral facing left. Climb the dihedral to a huge squared-off roof, where you can belay. Exit the roof rightward (5.9), layback around the outer corner, and face climb up to a big terrace halfway up the cliff. Roughly 30 feet of slab plus 100-plus feet from the dihedral foot.

Go straight up from the terrace toward a small roof, with decent gear to it. Above, either climb alarmingly run-out face to a flake belay, or trend up and right into the left-facing dihedral and belay at its top, which is better. Serious to very serious depending on line.
More face climbing to the foot of the white band. Belay there, or a few feet lower and left for a better stance. Between 150 and 200 feet.
Work up the white band's left flank, passing little acrobatic roofs and a shallow dihedral facing right, toward the top. The route's only fixed piton is in the first roof.
If pitch 6 used up the rope, finish to the top here. Serious.

review.changed: Wrote the 7 pitches the text describes. Lengths only where a single number is stated (P1, P2, P4). The text says pitches are probably longer than the guidebook gives and that many variations exist. No pitch 8 described.
review.other_findings: Stored pitch count is 8; text describes 7 and a 200 ft rope.

pitch_detail.notes: Reach the base by scrambling large ledges east of the long fin on the northeast ridge. The pitch can start from several places, all about 5.4 to 5.6, and uses roughly 160 feet of rope. Several belay spots are possible.

Similar 5.4-5.6 climbing straight up the ridge. After an opening 5.5 section and a long easy stretch, a short layback flake (under 10 feet) is the crux; belay on top of it. Staying left makes it easier, but go straight up. Veering left lets you belay on a dirt and grass ledge 30-50 feet below the flake instead.
Begin in a dihedral facing left, then go about straight up, or a touch right, via a chain of such dihedrals. The hardest move comes just under the belay. About 100-150 feet.

Easy ground up and slightly right, with a right-slanting finger crack near the top. Belay on the far side of the first bench on the route, beside the wide crack. A 60 m rope may allow linking with the next pitch.
Begins up a wide crack, though the face beside it is a pleasant way to avoid it. Easier than the lower pitches, and the line is obvious. Belay on a smaller ledge.
A little more loose rock and hollow-sounding holds, so go carefully. The summit is then an easy scramble, probably class 2.

review.changed: Wrote six pitches; grades only where stated (P1-P3). Crux flag left off P2 because the text names a flake crux but I kept it in the notes. Rappel table not written: the text gives 3 raps of 50-60 m but no per-station detail.
review.other_findings: Text notes some would count only 5 pitches since the last is near class 2.

pitch_detail.notes: Lead-in to Middle Earth Ledge. Several ways exist; the most direct is the first pitch of Sykes' Sickle.
Begins well right of the Eye of Mordor, the huge sinister vertical gouge left of centre on the east face. Easy going to a large ledge.
Straight into a clear dihedral that widens near the top. There is little gear late on unless you carry a very large piece; focused laybacking reaches the next big ledge.
Traverse left through a hole onto a ramp. Rather than going far along it, climb through an overhang or flake to the next ledge, which bends into a dihedral facing right.
Climb the dihedral, over a little roof, and hand-traverse left to a second short dihedral, belaying from slings high in it.

The crux section: a hand-width crack inside a small dihedral becomes a short finger crack running nearly sideways and then peters out under a smooth sweep of wall. Rearrange your feet to rock up onto a golden face of knobs, then reach a memorable flake and head right to a shallow dihedral with more hard moves. The usual belay is at that dihedral's base, but it can be linked with the next section for about 165 feet in all, which takes many runners. The upper section goes up the dihedral, breaks right onto more face climbing and a second shallow dihedral, belaying at its top.
Several dihedrals stacked above one another; stop at the top of the second.

The rock changes character but stays sound. Clip a bolt, ease left to a thin crack and place small stoppers, then follow it straight to the summit. As an alternative, descend left on 5.9 R face climbing to a dihedral and go up that.

review.changed: Wrote the pitches the text covers (P0-P7; the text repeats the exit pitch as an unlabelled P8 which I merged into P7). P1, P4 length and others unstated so omitted. Stored count is 11; text describes 8 plus the lead-in.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.11d; highest pitch grade in text is 5.11a/b.

pitch_detail.notes: Gentle slabs of ice, frequently thin and hard to protect. Clip the pin fixed in a right-hand crack for better placements. Belay on nuts and screws, depending on conditions, from a ledge beneath the steeper ice.
A handful of short, steep pillars, possibly hollow or chandeliered, with gentler ice between them. Finish on a ledge where the route becomes a steep snow climb.

Walk up steep snow with scarce protection toward a pillar of 70-85 degree ice. Place screws in the ice early; difficulty is low but exposure is serious. The slope steepens as it meets the pillar. Belay under the pillar on screws, or beneath the steepening snow using rock cracks.

Three choices: the main pillar, a shorter and steeper one to its right, or an escape left along a wide ledge of talus or snow. The main pillar gives smooth, thick ice and the best protection on the climb, though thin conditions make it hard to protect. It leads through a couloir to a notch, then left to the descent. The right-hand pillar finishes on rock before joining the top of the main one.

review.changed: Wrote all four pitches, no grades or lengths since none are given per pitch. Crux flag on P4 is an inference (steepest ice); remove if unwanted. (Reviewer: inferred crux flag removed.)

pitch_detail.notes: Start on a left-facing flake. High on it, move right into a v-groove and carry on over blocky face to Middle Earth Ledge. Many parties link this with pitch 2 or with pitches 2 and 3.
Third and fourth class: scramble to Middle Earth Ledge, then shift left.

Wander up the face to a slot leaning left and follow it out. The slot is optional; many parties instead belay from a fixed quicklink anchor and continue up flakes of mixed quality to the foot of the corner that faces right.

Move left across the face, then take the corner that faces right and belay as far up as you can. The ledge itself is fine, yet protection there is small and thin, so belaying beneath the corner has merit.
Complete the corner, then take the crack that leans left. It is easy to overshoot looking for a good stance.

Start left and go through the A-shaped roof, then up a lovely crack to a belay in a shallow corner that faces left; do not go too high. A shorter pitch, around 110-130 feet or less. Alternatively, from the alcove, a left-leaning corner runs about 30 feet, then the crack goes vertical and trends right to a ledge beneath the roof; after the roof belay on a ramp with small gear, or 20 feet higher with bigger gear in a semi-hanging stance.

Go up the corner, then the crack system until a seemingly sound piton appears in a crack angling right. Pass it for the short 5.10 crux, with insecure footholds, then a wider crack with good gear to where the headwall eases to a slab. Belay at the Barb Flake's crest, about 120 feet.

A crack breaks a small roof, then a ramp runs about 40 feet; step round the flake's edge at a tiny horn to reach the North Ridge route. Or take easy but run-out face to the flake's top and downclimb exposed and tricky to the notch.
Climb the North Ridge route's final two pitches to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 9 entries (P1-P8 plus the P9-10 North Ridge link). Alternate betas for P3, P6 and P7 were merged into one note each. Lengths only where given in feet.
review.other_findings: Text says some guidebooks grade the route up to 5.10c; stored is 5.10.

pitch_detail.notes: Strenuous but not very technical crack climbing, split between the right wall and the corner; extra hand-size cams help. Belay at a weak bolt and a mediocre ledge.
Keep going up the corner to a better ledge below the offwidth. Could be linked with the first pitch if gear allows, ideally with a second yellow Alien.

A slightly overhanging 5-6 inch crack in the corner, finishing on the pillar's top and a good ledge also used by Pervertical. Nearly all of it takes a #4.5 Camalot; a #4 is nearly useless and a #5 helps only at the end. Smaller gear fits in a left-hand crack, but placing it can block key handholds. A kneepad helps.
The last pitch of Pervertical, to Table Ledge. Belay about 40 feet south of the rappel anchors. Much easier than what came before.

review.changed: Wrote the four Obelisk pitches only; the two approach pitches via Window Direct and the Pervertical approach are not part of the table. Crux flag on P3 is an inference from the longest description and hardest gear needs. (Reviewer: inferred crux flag removed.)

pitch_detail.notes: Straight up the main weakness, skipping the second of the two left-hand bolts unless 5.10 face is your strength. Continue through a short chimney and offwidth section, then 10-20 feet higher move up a ramp to the left to a belay below the first small roof. Roughly 160 feet depending on which ledge you start from.

Go over a small roof and up the corner above. When it is easy to do so, traverse left onto the arete and follow its left side to the pine-tree ledge. Belay at the tree; this belay needs larger pieces (#2-3).

Step right into the first corner system at 5.9; the farther corner to the right is 5.10a. They meet at a bulge, which is the crux. Above, pass a second roof on its left and follow easier ground to the top, belaying at a hidden bolt or large trees.

review.changed: Wrote all three pitches. No rappel table (not described).

pitch_detail.notes: Begin on a small ledge 5 m right of the shallow crack that leans left and splits the face. Climb to the fourth bolt, make a bold step right, then good holds lead to a belay on a good ledge.
Easy ground first, then a face with plenty of big holds up to another ledge belay.
A short face and some sandy ledges to a comfortable ledge under an arch or overhang.
Layback the crack beneath the overhang, step right onto delicate face holds, then easy blocks lead into a corner. Belay on a good stance.
Up a corner using lots of footholds on it and the face, with sustained 5.9 moves, to a shady ledge that is a good place to rest before the headwall.
A few metres on interesting limestone, then traverse up and right with some gymnastic moves over the grassy ramp. Belay on a good stance.
Use an alpine draw on the third bolt and climb up and left onto a long ramp or dike that stays at 5.10a. Belay on a big ledge.
A short final slab up and right to a big grassy ledge, with bolts on the wall ahead. Can be linked with pitch 7.

review.changed: Wrote all 8 pitches with grade, length and bolt counts. Per-pitch anchors omitted: stations are three-bolt except one ledge, not stated per pitch. Not a rappel route (walk off).

pitch_detail.notes: Go up into a chimney that turns into an offwidth beneath a bulging roof. Clip a bolt, then either pull over the roof or face climb (both 5.8) to the next bolt, and trend right to an unprotected, airy 5.6 traverse to a pair of pins. With good rope drag, push on up the unprotected loose chimney to the bolted belay; otherwise belay at the pins with a backup. The one unpleasant pitch.

Continue into the loose chimney and around the corner, watching rope drag and clipping a bolt. Rock starts mediocre and becomes excellent grey limestone with edging past bolts that veer left. Mantle onto a scree ledge and belay at a massive bolted boulder.

Walk left from the previous belay along the path to a cairn between two small trees. Pull a low loose roof to reach solid rock; the 5.8 edging has little protection until a ledge. Go right into the obvious corner and belay from a block with a bolted anchor.

Flaring cracks with marginal protection lead to a block perched atop a pinnacle, then an airy traverse right on good holds toward a tall tree. Mantle up and belay in the nook holding a bolt and a fiddly crack system.
A looser cousin of the previous pitch, through a wide notch or else hard right up a grassy corner. Belay under the huge detached pinnacle.

Go up to the detached pinnacle, make wide moves (a big cam, or a rusty pin) and either grapple the wide crack or move out to the face, continuing to the pinnacle's top. Then aim for the bolt on the striking wall above: four bolts with almost no gear between them cover about half this 40 m pitch, on great edges and big ledge holds. Finish at a hanging bolt anchor close to a small ledge.
Good flared 5.8 corner climbing from the first move, with gear improving higher. Trend right beneath a little roof, make a short traverse onto easy grey stone and belay at bolts.

review.changed: Wrote all 7 pitches; grades only where stated. Lengths omitted except P6.

pitch_detail.notes: Start round the left-hand corner and make a brief climb to a bolted ledge belay.
Cracks and face climbing to a small ledge under the obvious right-facing corner.
Climb the corner, passing a little roof, to a bolted ledge belay. Watch for loose blocks.
Cracks straight above the belay lead to the summit. An easier option goes left at about 5.4 for 30 m.

review.changed: Wrote all 4 pitches. No rappel table: only 'rappel with a 60 m rope'.
review.other_findings: Pitch lengths sum to 90 m versus stored 107 m.

pitch_detail.notes: Leave the gully trending right, then left, to reach the first bolt about 10 m up. Bolts lead to a corner facing left, over a groove and a roof, ending at a station on the left beneath a small dirt ledge.
Head straight up beside a corner facing left to the large ledge, then past a ring-bolt rappel station, trending up and right to the following ledge and its station. Watch for loose rock on the ledge.

Climb the steep wall to an arete on the right, then a groove, and belay at the rappel station on the right. A two-bolt anchor sits 7 m higher, but the lower station gives better contact with your partner.
The first bolt is hard to spot, up and right of the alternative belay in a black band. Get over the steep bit and keep trending right to a large ledge, with the station beneath the roof.

Climb up and left past two bolts, then traverse left (long slings help) to a ledge with a small overhang. One 5.8 move straight up, or pull on a draw (A0), or step right at 5.6, the recommended option. Continue to a station well to the right.
Easy rock left of the station past one bolt, then straight up to a station on the right just below the ridge top.
A walk: pass right of the anchor, round behind the ridge and northwest to the main buttress, skirt it on the left and reach the foot of a fine wall with a bolt station facing the highway.
Up and left, then directly up the vertical wall to an alcove.
A short awkward chimney leads to a big sandy ledge, with a station on its right. Easily linked with the previous pitch.

Follow the groove up the central wall, with cracks on both sides, step around a roof by traversing left, and return right to a semi-hanging belay. The second bolt on the left traverse can be skipped to reduce drag.
Angle left up a groove, then right along bolts to a good ledge with a station.
Good rock and fine positions on the arete lead to a huge ledge with a station. Easily linked with the previous pitch.
Scramble roughly 10 m to the first bolt, then up and left around the arete on a small slab, passing ledges and a rappel station, to a station at the summit.

rappel_detail.notes: A short rappel from the summit ring bolts to the next station.
Rappel back down and round the arete on climber's right to a good ledge, then scramble down roughly 8 m to the anchor on the large ledge beneath.
Down to a station on a good ledge.
Down to the large sandy ledge.
A short rappel climber's left down the chimney crack to the alcove belay.
Down to the level ground at the foot of the upper mountain.
Not a rappel: walk round the buttress to the ridge's left side and find the station at the ridge end, on the right.
Rappel down and toward the right to the ledge beneath, to the station at the arete's edge.
From the edge station down to the next ledge, where the station hides under the roof.
Down to flatter ground, then walk back to the ring bolts near the edge.
Overhanging rappel to a big ledge with a station. Knot the rope ends; the pull is hard with lots of friction, but the rope does come down.
To the large ledge below; the station is at the far climber's left side.
To the small dirt ledge holding the pitch 2 ring-bolt station, directly below.
To the ground, then follow the cairns back.

review.changed: Wrote all 13 pitches and the rappel list. The source's rappel list numbers '13' twice, giving 15 steps; I numbered them 1-15 in order, and step 8 is a walk, not a rappel.

pitch_detail.notes: Steep ice, sometimes hollow, up to a fixed belay on the left.
More steep ice up to the broad ledge, where a fixed anchor waits. Can sound hollow where ice separates from the wall, and may be thin near the top.
Shift the belay up and right, then a brief pitch to a fixed anchor tucked in a protected alcove.
A lengthy, steep pitch of quality ice to the top, finishing at a fixed anchor on the right. The hardest pitch.

review.changed: Wrote four pitches, no grades or lengths (not given). No rappel table: only 'rappel from fixed stations'.

pitch_detail.notes: Steep ice, often thin, up to a bolted station on the right that may be iced over.

pitch_detail.anchor: bolted station, alcove on the right
pitch_detail.notes: A steep pillar, then easy ice to the alcove.
A sequence of ice steps leads to a further station on the right.
More ice and some snow, finishing at a station on the left.
A long pitch on WI3-4 ice, then a 20 m traverse into small trees for an anchor. Simul-climbing may be needed.
Plough across and up the steep snow slope and belay at the foot of the last ice, then 75-degree ice to a station left. Not visible until you top out pitch 5.

review.changed: Wrote all 6 pitches with lengths. No rappel table: the descent is described in grouped terms (one rap, then three more skipping some anchors), not station by station.
review.other_findings: Stored 305 m; pitch lengths sum to 250 m.

pitch_detail.notes: Bolted slab pitch of about 25 m at 5.8, the easiest of the four.
Bolted pitch of about 25 m at 5.10c, carrying the route's grade.
Bolted pitch of about 25 m at 5.10a.
Bolted pitch of about 25 m at 5.9 to finish. A dozen draws are enough, or 16 if linking pitches.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches with grade and length only; the source gives nothing else per pitch, so notes are minimal. No rappels or bolt counts stated.

pitch_detail.notes: The first bolt is high, around 6 m up, and the climbing then gets harder, up to about 5.10c.
Sustained steep 5.10 climbing, harder than the first pitch, with a 5.10c crux.
Two harder roof sections keep up the sustained character of the route.
Fewer sustained moves than before, but a few hard ones and a traverse. Long draws help.
More low-5.10 climbing to a ledge, above which the rock is less good.
The route's hardest pitch, a steep boulder-problem crux. Do not top out: the rock above is loose, so rappel from here.

review.changed: Wrote all 6 pitches. No rappel table: only that it is rigged for 35 m rappels and the last two stations differ from the belays, with no list.

pitch_detail.notes: Bolted south-facing slab of about 25 m at 5.9.
Bolted pitch of about 25 m at 5.10b, the hardest of the route.
Bolted pitch of about 25 m at 5.8, the easiest of the four.
Bolted pitch of about 25 m at 5.10a to finish. Linking pitches is possible but rope drag builds; bring 16 draws if so.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches with grade and length only; notes minimal because the source has nothing more per pitch. No rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: A steep first step that eases to a belay on ice before the snow slope. Then slog about 70 m up the snow to the main ice.

Good ice leads to a cave on the right, where a bolted station sits behind the pillar. If the cave is blocked, hack back to it or accept a hanging belay. Parties with 70 m ropes can keep going up the pillar and belay from its top.
The steep crux pillar, then easier rambling ice and one last steep step to the top.

review.changed: Wrote all 3 pitches. No rappel table: 'rappel on V-threads' only.

pitch_detail.notes: Good holds up a short corner facing right, traverse left onto easy ground in a bigger right-facing corner, then edge up and left through a crack to a broad ledge system.

Move left about 30 feet along the big ledge (a small cairn marks it), then up blocky ground. After roughly 70 feet, go left a few moves to a slab with shallow vertical cracks, follow them up and left, then traverse right to the station beneath a small roof.
Right, then up good holds with three bolts, then easy fourth-class ground. You can build a midway station, or simul-climb to the station beneath a black groove or chimney.
Up the black groove with simple route-finding. The white corner on the left reaches the same point.
Move slightly right, then up along obvious weaknesses, left beneath a wide crack, and through a little overhang to a wooded ledge.
Hike up and left along a trail, then scramble back right up an obvious ramp onto a big ledge. A few more low fifth-class moves left reach the final headwall.

From the far left end of the final ledge, above a square-cut boulder, go up cracks and through a slot to beneath a roof, shift right around it, then back left into a steep corner system leaning right and follow it to the top.

review.changed: Wrote all 7 pitches with grade and length (feet to metres). Anchors only where stated: stations are bolted on all but the last two pitches. Grade tokens like 5.6- recorded as 5.6.

skip_reasons.ut_question_mark_wall_route: Text describes 4 pitches with aid grades (A1) and a 5.8+ R free pitch, but the stored row says 3 pitches and 5.12b; the mismatch makes it doubtful this is the same route, so skipped.
